lessons.title: Principles of Avocado Pruning
lessons.body:
Pruning is not just cutting branches; it is directing the tree's energy to where you want it. In avocado, the goal is to grow a tree with a strong central leader, well-spaced branches, and a canopy that captures sunlight without becoming too dense. Avocado trees are naturally tall and upright, so without pruning they become lanky, with fruit only at the top. Pruning keeps the tree at a manageable height (4-5 meters) for easy harvesting and spraying.

There are three main types of pruning: training young trees, maintenance pruning for light, and rejuvenation of old trees. Each has a different purpose. Training shapes the tree early; maintenance removes crowded branches; rejuvenation brings back productivity in old trees. Always prune with a purpose: remove dead, diseased, or broken branches first, then thin out crowded areas, then head back long branches to encourage branching.

Timing matters. In Africa, prune during the dry season when the tree is not actively flushing or fruiting. Avoid pruning during heavy rains to reduce disease risk. The best time is just after harvest, before the next flowering. For most regions, this is between June and August. Pruning during flowering or fruiting can reduce yield and stress the tree.

Remember the 3 D's: Dead, Diseased, and Damaged. Remove these first. Then look for branches that cross or rub, and remove one. Also remove water sprouts (vigorous vertical shoots) that grow from the trunk or main branchesâthey sap energy and block light. Aim for a canopy that is open enough that you can see light patches on the ground. A well-pruned avocado tree will produce more fruit, larger fruit, and be easier to manage. Always use clean, sharp tools to make clean cuts that heal quickly. Never leave stubs; cut just outside the branch collar (the swollen area where branch meets trunk).

lessons.title: Training Young Trees
lessons.body:
Training a young avocado tree starts from planting. Your goal is to develop a strong framework of 3-4 main branches (scaffolds) spaced evenly around the trunk, starting at about 60-80 cm above the ground. This allows air and light into the center and makes harvesting easy. If you let the tree grow naturally, it will become tall and narrow, with fruit only at the top.

In the first year, allow the tree to grow undisturbed to establish roots. In the second year, select 3-4 strong, well-spaced branches to become the main scaffolds. Remove all other branches below and between them. Cut them flush with the trunk. If the tree has a central leader, cut it back to about 1 meter to force branching. Use a sharp pair of secateurs (hand pruners) for small branches and a pruning saw for larger ones. Always make cuts at a slight angle, just above a bud or branch.

In the third year, continue shaping. Remove any branches that grow inward, cross, or rub. Keep the center open. Head back the main scaffolds by about one-third to encourage side shoots. This will create a rounded, spreading canopy. Do not prune too heavily; remove no more than 25% of the canopy in one year. Young trees are easily stunted by over-pruning.

In Africa, many farmers intercrop avocados with bananas or coffee. Ensure your pruning does not shade these crops excessively. Also, train the tree to a height that allows you to reach most fruit with a ladder. A well-trained tree will start bearing in 3-4 years and will be productive for decades. Remember to remove any suckers that grow from the rootstock below the graft union. These are from the rootstock and will not produce the same fruit. Cut them off as soon as you see them.

lessons.title: Pruning for Light Management
lessons.body:
Light is the key to fruit production. Avocado trees need at least 6 hours of direct sunlight per day. When the canopy becomes too dense, the inside of the tree is shaded, and fruit production drops. The goal of light management pruning is to create a canopy that is open enough to allow sunlight to penetrate to the inner branches, but not so open that it exposes fruit to sunburn.

Start by removing any branches that are growing straight up (water sprouts) and any that are crossing or rubbing. These block light and cause damage. Then, thin out the canopy by removing selected branches, especially those that are more than 2 cm in diameter. Aim to remove about 20-30% of the canopy each year. A good rule of thumb: after pruning, you should be able to see dappled light on the ground under the tree.

Use the 'three-cut method' for larger branches to avoid tearing bark. First, make a cut on the underside of the branch about 30 cm from the trunk, going about one-third through. Second, make a cut on the top side, slightly further out, until the branch falls. Third, cut the remaining stub back to the branch collar. This prevents bark stripping and allows quick healing.

In Africa, where many avocado orchards are in high-altitude areas with strong sun, be careful not to over-prune. Sudden exposure of previously shaded branches can cause sunburn, which leads to disease. Prune gradually over 2-3 years. Also, remove any branches that are touching the ground; they can harbor pests and diseases. Keep the skirt of the tree about 50 cm above the ground. After pruning, the tree will redirect energy to the remaining branches, producing more fruit and better quality.

lessons.title: Rejuvenation Pruning of Mature Trees
lessons.body:
Mature avocado trees that have been neglected or are too tall can be rejuvenated. Rejuvenation pruning involves cutting back the tree severely to stimulate new growth and restore productivity. This is done on trees that are 10 years or older, have become too tall (over 6 meters), or have many dead branches and low yields.

The best time to rejuvenate is after harvest, during the dry season. Use a pruning saw and loppers. Start by removing all dead, diseased, and broken branches. Then, decide on the height you want. For most farmers, a height of 4-5 meters is manageable. Cut back the main branches to that height, making cuts just above a strong side branch or bud. Do not cut into the old wood too much; leave some branches for regrowth.

After the initial cut, the tree will produce many new shoots. In the following year, select 4-6 strong shoots to become the new main branches. Remove the rest. Continue to shape the tree over the next 2-3 years. It may take 2-3 years for the tree to return to full production, but the fruit will be easier to harvest and of better quality.

Rejuvenation is stressful for the tree. To help it recover, apply fertilizer (e.g., 200 g of NPK 17-17-17 per tree) and mulch around the base. Ensure adequate watering during dry spells. Do not rejuvenate more than one-third of your orchard in a single year, so you maintain some income. Also, be aware that severe pruning can expose the trunk to sunburn; paint the exposed branches with white latex paint diluted 1:1 with water to reflect sunlight. This simple step can save your tree from dieback.

lessons.title: Tools and Techniques for Pruning
lessons.body:
Using the right tools makes pruning easier and safer for both you and the tree. You need: a pair of bypass secateurs (hand pruners) for branches up to 2 cm, a lopper for branches up to 5 cm, and a pruning saw for larger branches. Always keep them sharp and clean. Sharp tools make clean cuts that heal fast; dull tools crush stems and invite disease. Clean your tools with methylated spirits or bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) between trees to prevent spreading diseases like avocado sunblotch viroid.

Techniques: For small branches, cut at a 45-degree angle about 5 mm above an outward-facing bud. This encourages growth in the direction you want. For larger branches, use the three-cut method to prevent bark tearing. First, cut on the underside about 30 cm from the trunk, one-third through. Second, cut from the top, slightly further out, until the branch falls. Third, cut the stub back to the branch collar (the swollen ring where branch meets trunk). Never leave a stub; it will die back and invite disease.

When removing a branch, support it with your free hand to avoid tearing. For tall branches, use a pole pruner or a ladder. Never prune from a ladder while holding a saw; use both hands. Wear gloves and eye protection. In Africa, many farmers use machetes or pangas, but these cause ragged cuts and should be avoided for pruning. Invest in good tools; they will last for years.

After pruning, disinfect your tools again before moving to the next tree. Also, sharpen your tools regularly with a file or sharpening stone. A well-maintained tool is a pleasure to use and ensures the health of your trees.

lessons.title: Disposal of Pruning Debris
lessons.body:
After pruning, you will have a pile of branches and leaves. How you dispose of this debris affects the health of your orchard. Diseased branches should be burned or removed from the farm immediately. Do not compost them, as pathogens can survive and spread. For healthy branches and leaves, you can compost them or use them as mulch. Composting kills many pathogens if done properly (turn the pile and ensure it heats up to 55-60Â°C).

Mulching with pruned material is beneficial. Chipped branches and leaves can be spread around the base of the tree, but keep them 10-15 cm away from the trunk to prevent collar rot. Mulch conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and adds organic matter. However, if the branches are from a tree with root rot (Phytophthora), do not use them as mulch around healthy trees; burn them instead.

In Africa, many farmers use pruning debris for firewood or fencing. This is fine, but be aware that moving debris to other areas can spread pests and diseases. If you use branches for firewood, stack them away from the orchard. Never leave piles of debris in the orchard; they harbor pests like fruit flies and rodents. Also, do not dump debris in waterways, as it can block streams and cause erosion.

A good practice is to have a designated area for burning diseased material. Burn when there is no wind and ensure the fire is completely out before leaving. For large branches, consider renting a chipper if you have many trees. The chips can be used as mulch or compost. Proper disposal is part of good orchard hygiene. It reduces disease pressure and keeps your farm neat and productive.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pruning and Canopy Management for Avocado Farming in Africa

Pruning is the highest-return management investment an avocado grower can make after irrigation and nutrition. In African production systemsâwhether smallholder orchards in Kenya's Murang'a County, commercial blocks in South Africa's Limpopo, or emerging estates in Tanzania and Ethiopiaâcanopy management directly determines fruit size, pack-out percentage, pest pressure, and harvest labour costs. This practical reference consolidates the operational knowledge from the six lessons in this module into field-ready guidance.

Avocado (Persea americana) is an evergreen, indeterminate tree. Unlike deciduous fruit trees, it does not have a true dormant period, which means pruning must be timed carefully to avoid removing productive wood or exposing bark to sunburn. The tree flowers on terminal and sub-terminal shoots from the previous season's growth, so understanding the relationship between pruning intensity and flowering is central to profitable management.

Why Pruning Pays: The Business Case

Unpruned avocado trees in African orchards typically develop tall, narrow canopies with fruit concentrated in the top third. This creates three profit leaks: (1) harvest labour costs rise because pickers need ladders and more time per tree; (2) fruit size drops because inner canopy leaves shade out lower fruiting sites; and (3) pest and disease pressure increases because airflow is restricted, favouring anthracnose and fruit fly. A well-managed canopy can lift export-grade pack-out from 45â55% to 70â80% within two seasons, which at Kenyan farm-gate prices of KES 80â120 per kilogram for export Hass translates to significant additional revenue per hectare.

Timing Pruning in African Growing Conditions

In Kenya, Tanzania, and Ethiopia, the main pruning window is immediately after harvest (typically JuneâAugust for the main crop) and before the next flowering flush. In South Africa, pruning is done in late winter to early spring (AugustâSeptember) to avoid the hot, humid summer months when wounds are vulnerable to infection. In all regions, avoid pruning during active flowering or fruit set, as this stresses the tree and reduces yield.

Table 1: Recommended pruning windows by African avocado-producing region
Region / Country Main Pruning Window Secondary Window Reason
Kenya (Central Highlands) JuneâAugust JanuaryâFebruary (light) Post-harvest; avoids flowering peak
Tanzania (Kilimanjaro, Mbeya) JulyâSeptember February (light) Post-harvest; dry season wound healing
South Africa (Limpopo, Mpumalanga) AugustâSeptember FebruaryâMarch (light) Avoids humid summer disease pressure
Ethiopia (Yirgacheffe, Sidama) JuneâAugust January (light) Post-harvest; dry season
Rwanda / Burundi JulyâSeptember February (light) Post-harvest; cooler dry period

Source: Compiled from Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) Avocado Production Manual (2021); South African Avocado Growers' Association (SAAGA) Technical Guidelines; FAO Avocado Production and Post-Harvest Handling Guide (2019).

Training Young Trees (Years 1â4)

The goal in the first four years is to build a strong framework that will support heavy crops without breaking. Start by selecting a central leader and 3â4 well-spaced scaffold branches at 45â60Â° angles. Remove competing leaders and any branches below 50 cm from the ground. In the second year, head back the central leader to encourage branching and remove inward-growing or crossing branches. By year four, the tree should have a balanced, open canopy with light reaching the inner fruiting zone.

In African conditions, young trees are often intercropped with beans, maize, or vegetables. Pruning must account for this: avoid shading intercrops excessively, but do not over-prune young trees, as this delays canopy development and delays first commercial harvest.

Pruning for Light Management in Mature Trees

Light is the currency of fruit production. Avocado leaves need at least 30% of full sunlight to photosynthesise efficiently. In a mature orchard, the canopy should be managed so that dappled light reaches the ground beneath the tree. This is achieved by:

  • Thinning cuts: Remove entire branches back to the trunk or a main scaffold to open the canopy.
  • Heading cuts: Shorten long, leggy branches to encourage side shoots and fruiting wood.
  • Skirting: Remove low-hanging branches that touch the ground or interfere with irrigation and harvest.
  • Window pruning: Remove selected branches to create light channels into the canopy interior.
â  SAFETY WARNING â Chainsaw and Pole Pruner Use

Pruning avocado trees involves working at height with sharp tools. In African orchards, chainsaw injuries and falls from ladders are among the most common serious farm accidents. Always wear a helmet, eye protection, ear defenders, cut-resistant gloves, and steel-toed boots. Never use a chainsaw above shoulder height. Ensure ladders are on firm, level ground and secured. Keep a first-aid kit and mobile phone within reach. Do not work alone. If using a pole pruner near power lines, maintain a minimum 10-metre clearance and contact the utility provider before starting.

Rejuvenation Pruning of Mature Trees

Many African avocado orchards contain trees over 15 years old that have become too tall, too dense, or have suffered storm or disease damage. Rejuvenation pruning restores productivity by removing old, unproductive wood and stimulating new growth. The process is gradual: over two to three seasons, remove 25â30% of the canopy per year, starting with the tallest central leaders and the most congested inner branches. Never remove more than one-third of the canopy in a single season, as this exposes the trunk to sunburn and can cause dieback.

Table 2: Pruning intensity guide for mature avocado trees
Tree Condition Pruning Intensity Timing Expected Recovery
Healthy, productive (10â15 yrs) Light maintenance (10â15% canopy) Post-harvest Immediate
Slightly congested (15â20 yrs) Moderate thinning (20â25% canopy) Post-harvest, dry season 1 season
Overgrown / low yield (20+ yrs) Rejuvenation (25â30% per year over 2â3 years) Post-harvest, early dry season 2â3 seasons
Storm / disease damaged Corrective (remove damaged wood only) Immediately after damage 1â2 seasons

Source: Adapted from KALRO Avocado Production Manual (2021) and University of California Cooperative Extension Avocado Canopy Management (2018), validated for African conditions by SAAGA.

Tools and Techniques

African avocado growers use a range of tools depending on orchard size and budget. Smallholders typically use hand saws, loppers, and secateurs, while commercial estates use pneumatic pruners, pole pruners, and chainsaws. Regardless of tool, the principles are the same: make clean cuts at the branch collar, do not leave stubs, and sterilise tools between trees to prevent disease spread.

  • Secateurs: For branches up to 2 cm diameter.
  • Loppers: For branches 2â4 cm diameter.
  • Pruning saw: For branches 4â10 cm diameter.
  • Pole pruner: For high branches up to 6 cm diameter.
  • Chainsaw: For branches over 10 cm diameter; use only with proper training and PPE.

Always cut at a slight angle away from the bud, leaving a smooth surface. For large cuts (over 5 cm), apply a wound sealant or fungicide paint to prevent infection, especially in humid African conditions where anthracnose and Phytophthora are prevalent.

Disposal of Pruning Debris

Pruning debris is not wasteâit is a resource and a disease risk. In African orchards, debris left on the ground can harbour fruit fly, anthracnose spores, and Phytophthora. Best practice is to:

  • Chop debris into small pieces and compost it away from the orchard.
  • Use healthy wood chips as mulch around trees (but not touching the trunk).
  • Burn or remove diseased material immediatelyâdo not compost it.
  • Never leave large branches on the ground near the tree base, as they attract termites and rodents.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Timing: Prune immediately after harvest, before flowering. Avoid wet, humid periods.
  2. Tools: Use sharp, clean tools. Sterilise between trees with 70% alcohol or bleach solution.
  3. Young trees: Select 3â4 scaffold branches, remove competing leaders, head back central leader.
  4. Mature trees: Remove no more than 25â30% of canopy per season. Prioritise light penetration.
  5. Cuts: Make clean cuts at the branch collar. No stubs. Seal cuts over 5 cm.
  6. Safety: Wear PPE. Never chainsaw above shoulder height. Work with a partner.
  7. Debris: Remove diseased wood. Compost healthy material away from orchard.
  8. Record: Note pruning dates, intensity, and tree response for future planning.

Further Reading

  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization: Avocado Production Manual
  • South African Avocado Growers' Association (SAAGA) â Technical Guidelines
  • FAO â Good Agricultural Practices for Avocado Production and Post-Harvest Handling
  • AvocadoSource â University of California Avocado Canopy Management Resources
  • Purdue University â Avocado Horticulture and Pruning Guides

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. For practical demonstrations, contact your local agricultural extension officer or KALRO/SAAGA representative.

quiz.q: What is the primary goal of pruning an avocado tree?
options: A) To make the tree look attractive
B) To direct the tree's energy for better fruit production and manageability
C) To reduce the number of trees in an orchard
D) To increase the height of the tree
quiz.explanation: Pruning directs energy to produce a strong framework and open canopy for better fruit yield and easier management.

quiz.q: When is the best time to prune avocado trees in Africa?
options: C) During the dry season after harvest
D) At any time of year
quiz.explanation: Pruning during the dry season after harvest minimizes stress and disease risk.

quiz.q: What are the '3 D's' to remove first when pruning?
quiz.explanation: The 3 D's are Dead, Diseased, and Damaged branches, which should be removed first.

quiz.q: How many main scaffold branches should you aim for when training a young avocado tree?
quiz.explanation: 3-4 well-spaced main branches create a strong, open framework.

quiz.q: At what height above the ground should the first main branches be selected?
quiz.explanation: Starting branches at 60-80 cm allows for easy harvesting and air circulation.

quiz.q: What is the maximum percentage of canopy you should remove when pruning a young tree?
quiz.explanation: Removing more than 25% can stunt young trees.

quiz.q: What should you do with suckers growing from the rootstock below the graft union?
options: B) Cut them off as soon as seen
C) Graft them to the main tree
D) Tie them to the trunk
quiz.explanation: Suckers from the rootstock will not produce the desired fruit and sap energy.

quiz.q: Why is light management important in avocado pruning?
options: B) To allow sunlight to reach inner branches for fruit production
D) To reduce the need for fertilizer
quiz.explanation: Sunlight penetration is essential for fruit bud formation and quality.

quiz.q: What is the 'three-cut method' used for?
options: B) Removing large branches without tearing bark
quiz.explanation: The three-cut method prevents bark stripping when removing large branches.

quiz.q: How much of the canopy should be removed annually in light management pruning?
quiz.explanation: Removing 20-30% opens the canopy without over-exposing branches.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your avocado tree needs rejuvenation pruning?
options: A) The tree is 2 years old
B) The tree is over 6 meters tall and has low yields
C) The tree has many new shoots
D) The tree is bearing too much fruit
quiz.explanation: Rejuvenation is for mature, neglected, or too-tall trees with declining productivity.

quiz.q: After rejuvenation pruning, how long might it take for the tree to return to full production?
quiz.explanation: It takes 2-3 years for the tree to regrow and bear fruit again.

quiz.q: What should you apply to exposed branches after severe pruning to prevent sunburn?
options: B) White latex paint diluted with water
quiz.explanation: White paint reflects sunlight and protects exposed bark from sunburn.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for cutting branches up to 2 cm in diameter?
quiz.explanation: Bypass secateurs are designed for small branches and make clean cuts.

quiz.q: Why should you clean your pruning tools between trees?
options: C) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Cleaning with disinfectant prevents transmission of pathogens like avocado sunblotch viroid.

quiz.q: What is the correct angle for cutting a small branch?
quiz.explanation: A 45-degree angle just above a bud promotes healing and outward growth.

quiz.q: What is the branch collar?
options: A) The tip of the branch
B) The swollen area where branch meets trunk
quiz.explanation: The branch collar contains cells that help the tree heal after a cut.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a machete for pruning?
options: B) It causes ragged cuts that heal poorly
D) It is not allowed in orchards
quiz.explanation: Machetes crush stems, leading to disease and slow healing.

quiz.q: How should you dispose of diseased pruning debris?
options: C) Burn it or remove from farm
D) Leave it in the orchard
quiz.explanation: Burning or removing diseased material prevents spread of pathogens.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching with healthy pruning debris?
options: B) It conserves moisture and suppresses weeds
D) It makes the orchard messy
quiz.explanation: Mulch improves soil health and reduces water loss.

quiz.q: How far should mulch be kept from the tree trunk?
quiz.explanation: Keeping mulch away from the trunk prevents collar rot.

quiz.q: What should you do with pruning debris from a tree with root rot?
options: A) Use as mulch around healthy trees
D) Leave it on the ground
quiz.explanation: Root rot pathogens can survive in debris and spread, so burning is safest.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove water sprouts?
options: A) They produce the best fruit
B) They sap energy and block light
C) They are needed for structure
quiz.explanation: Water sprouts are vigorous vertical shoots that divert energy and shade the canopy.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for the skirt of the tree (lowest branches) above ground?
quiz.explanation: Keeping branches 50 cm above ground reduces pest and disease problems.

quiz.q: What is the maximum percentage of trees in an orchard that should be rejuvenated in one year?
quiz.explanation: Rejuvenating no more than one-third maintains some income while renewing the orchard.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is recommended after rejuvenation pruning?
quiz.explanation: Balanced NPK helps the tree recover and produce new growth.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of leaving a stub when pruning?
options: A) It helps the tree heal
B) It invites disease and dieback
D) It is necessary for support
quiz.explanation: Stubs die back and can become entry points for pathogens.

quiz.q: What should you do with pruning debris if you want to use it as firewood?
options: A) Leave it in the orchard
B) Stack it away from the orchard
quiz.explanation: Stacking away from the orchard prevents pest and disease spread.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pruning during heavy rains?
options: A) It is too wet to work
B) Wet conditions increase disease risk
C) The tree will grow too fast
quiz.explanation: Rain splashes can spread fungal and bacterial diseases to fresh cuts.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of training a young avocado tree?
options: A) It makes the tree grow taller
B) It creates a strong framework for future production
C) It reduces the need for water
quiz.explanation: Training shapes the tree for easy management and high yields.
